subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites students to share one thing they try to finish before starting something new, drawing out the everyday experience of focus and task-completion.
The teacher reads the poem aloud at a measured pace, pointing to each stanza in the textbook. The read-aloud is repeated once, with students following along silently on their copies.

The teacher reads a third time, pausing after each stanza to invite students to repeat the lines chorally. Emphasis falls on the natural rhythm and the refrain 'work while you work, and play while you play'.
Students take turns reading the poem aloud in pairs — one stanza each. The teacher listens and gently corrects phrasing, keeping the mood encouraging and unhurried.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem has four identical-length stanzas and a recurring refrain, making it well-suited to repeated reading at varied pace. Students may rush the refrain because it sounds familiar; slow them down by modelling a deliberate pause after each pair of lines.

periods.activity_title: Reading to Understand — Meaning and Rhyme

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (pp. 36): discuss focus, rhyme-pairs, feelings after task-completion.

time_bands.activity: Having heard the poem read aloud, students and teacher recite the first two stanzas together once, refreshing the language before discussion.

Let us Think — A. (p. 36): the teacher poses questions 1 and 3 — why focus matters, and how finishing a task feels — opening each to whole-class paired talk before drawing out a shared class response.

Let us Think — A. (p. 36): students skim the poem to collect rhyming word-pairs (question 2) and share them aloud. The teacher lists the pairs on the board: play/way, might/right, well/tell, away/play.
Let us Think — A. (p. 36): question 4 — students share daily practices that help them stay focused. The teacher summarises two or three responses to close the discussion.

periods.teacher_notes: Questions 1 and 3 are personal and reflective; students may give one-word answers. Prompt fuller responses by asking 'What happens when we don't focus?' and 'Can you say a little more about that feeling?' The rhyme-collection in question 2 doubles as phonics awareness — note the pair away/play echoes play/way from stanza 1, reinforcing the refrain's structure.

periods.activity_title: Talk About Free Time and Picture Sentences

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — B. (p. 36): guided discussion on favourite free-time activities.
Let us Speak (p. 37): describe activities in the Madhubani painting using Who–Is/Are–Doing What structure.

time_bands.activity: Let us Think — B. (p. 36): the teacher asks 'What do you like doing in your free time?' Students share with a partner first, then three or four pairs report to the class. The teacher draws out the work/play contrast the poem explores.

Let us Speak (p. 37): teacher draws students' attention to the Madhubani painting in the textbook and leads a picture walk — naming each activity visible, eliciting observations ('Who do you see? What are they doing?').

Let us Speak (p. 37): the teacher models two sentences using the Who–Is/Are–Doing What frame ('Two girls are going to school. A woman is typing on a computer.'). Students compose three sentences orally in pairs using the frame, then share aloud.
Pairs share their sentences with the class. The teacher offers brief corrective feedback on subject-verb agreement and prompts variety by pointing to unmentioned parts of the painting.

periods.teacher_notes: The Madhubani painting shows simultaneous activities — farming, dancing, cooking, swimming — which naturally models the poem's theme of purposeful engagement. Some students may produce single-word responses in the picture walk; the sentence frame keeps everyone producing full utterances. Seven written sentences are a textbook follow-up; oral production is the focus here.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — A. (p. 36): match poem vocabulary — might, useful, moments — to meanings.

homework.task_brief: Let us Listen (p. 39): circle words from the list where the 'l' is silent — calm, palm, calf, chalk, talk, balm — after practising the word list at home.

time_bands.activity: Let us Learn — A. (p. 36): the teacher writes 'might', 'useful', and 'moments' on the board and asks students where each appears in the poem. Students locate the lines and read them aloud to establish context.

Let us Learn — A. (p. 36): students work in pairs to match the three words to their meanings from the textbook ('strength or power', 'helpful or beneficial', 'short periods of time'). The teacher facilitates by prompting — 'Which line uses might? What is happening in that line?'
Pairs share their matches. The teacher confirms correct answers and invites students to use each word in a new oral sentence — away from the poem context — to consolidate meaning.

Brief consolidation: the teacher reads a sentence aloud with one of the three words used correctly and one used in a playful wrong context; students thumbs-up or thumbs-down to signal correctness, explaining their choice in one sentence.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often conflate 'might' (strength) with 'might' as a modal verb — both meanings are valid in English and the poem uses the noun. Accept the modal meaning if a student raises it, and briefly note that same spelling can carry two meanings. The silent-l task is assigned for home listening practice; it will be revisited in class.

periods.activity_title: The Case of Missing L — Phonics Listening

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen (p. 39): circle words where the 'l' is silent — teacher reads 15-word list aloud.

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes 'calm' and 'leaf' on the board and asks students to say each aloud. Guide them to notice that the 'l' in 'calm' disappears in speech while the 'l' in 'leaf' is heard clearly — this frames the silent-l concept before the drill.

Let us Listen (p. 39): the teacher reads the 15-word list — leaf, calm, pale, jail, palm, hall, clean, calf, shelf, chalk, talk, silk, balm, plum, self — aloud, word by word, at a clear pace with three full repetitions. Students circle words where the 'l' is not heard.

The teacher reads the list a final time while students verify their circles. The class then says each silent-l word aloud together — calm, palm, calf, chalk, talk, balm — exaggerating the missing-l pronunciation to make the pattern physical.
Students pair up: one partner reads any five words from the list and the other signals thumbs-up if the 'l' is silent, thumbs-down if heard. Pairs swap roles for the second five.

periods.teacher_notes: The six silent-l words in this list — calm, palm, calf, chalk, talk, balm — follow the pattern where 'l' after a vowel before certain consonants is unpronounced. Students from regional-language backgrounds may pronounce every letter; reassure them that silent letters are a feature of English spelling, not a reading error. Model each silent-l word twice before the paired practice.

periods.activity_title: My Daily Routine — Table and Draft

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write (pp. 38–39): fill in personal daily-routine table, classifying each activity as work or play.
Let us Write (pp. 38–39): write daily routine as a structured paragraph using the three-part frame provided.

time_bands.activity: The teacher models filling in the daily-routine table on the board with their own (or a fictional student's) routine — writing three rows, ticking work or play for each, and thinking aloud about the choice ('Getting dressed — is it work or play? Why?').

Let us Write (pp. 38–39): students fill in the six-row table in the textbook with their own daily activities and tick the work or play column. The teacher circulates, prompting students who leave rows blank to think about morning or after-school time.

Let us Write (pp. 38–39): the teacher reads the three paragraph frames aloud — My Routine, At School, At Home — and models completing two blanks of the first frame on the board. Students use their table to fill in the frames in their notebooks, beginning with the morning frame.

Two or three volunteers read their completed morning-frame paragraphs aloud. The teacher offers specific praise on accurate time expressions and gently corrects any subject-verb mismatches, writing the correct form on the board without singling students out.

periods.teacher_notes: The table-to-paragraph sequence asks students to first classify their day and then narrate it — two genuinely different cognitive tasks. Keep the table phase brisk so the paragraph frame gets adequate time; the frame's blanks are the key writing event. The 'At Home' frame has open lines rather than blanks, which gives Grade IV students a small stretch toward freer writing.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do — A. (p. 41): guess the three riddles and explain the reasoning aloud.

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks students: 'What is a riddle?' After brief responses, the teacher explains that a riddle hides its answer inside clues — the fun is reading the clues carefully rather than guessing fast. This frames patient, focused reading, echoing the poem's own message.

Let us Do — A. (p. 41): the teacher reads Riddle 1 (Thirty white horses) aloud twice slowly, then invites students to think in silence for a moment before raising a hand. Volunteers share guesses; the teacher asks 'What clue told you?' before confirming the answer: teeth.

Let us Do — A. (p. 41): Riddle 2 (Tall lady / in a white frock) is read aloud. Students confer in pairs before sharing. The teacher unpacks the imagery — 'frock' as the candle's wax, 'yellow face' as the flame, 'grows shorter' as it melts — drawing out how figurative language creates the puzzle.

Let us Do — A. (p. 41): Riddle 3 (Hard and brown outside) is read aloud. Students write their guess on a slip of paper and hold it up together. The teacher confirms the answer (coconut) and invites students to invent one short clue of their own for a familiar object, sharing orally in the final minutes.

periods.teacher_notes: The three riddles progress from body (teeth) to object (candle) to food (coconut), building confidence. Students who guess immediately often skip the clue-justification step; insist on 'What in the riddle told you?' to develop careful reading. Inviting students to create their own one-line clue at the end strengthens the creative and linguistic payoff.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do — B. (p. 41–42): draw or paste holiday activities and describe them aloud to the class.

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites students to name one activity they truly enjoy during holidays — no textbook; just a quick oral round-the-class. Two or three students share briefly, with the teacher noting the variety on the board.

Let us Do — B. (pp. 41–42): students use the textbook space to draw one or two holiday activities they enjoy. Those who prefer it may sketch quickly and add colour; the teacher circulates to encourage detail and label suggestions.

Students take turns holding up their drawing and describing it in two or three sentences — 'I drew myself swimming. I love it because...' The teacher models the first description to lower the speaking threshold.

Brief whole-class reflection: the teacher asks 'Looking at everyone's pictures, what do you notice about play?' — eliciting variety, joy, and the idea that play done wholeheartedly is its own kind of effort, linking back to the poem's message.

periods.teacher_notes: This activity is genuinely creative and personal; resist the urge to evaluate drawings. The speaking moment ('describe your drawing') is the key language outcome. Students who are shy about their drawing can be invited to describe in words first and draw after; the constitution bans dependence on prior artefacts, so no prior product is needed or expected.

periods.activity_title: Recite, Reflect, and Revisit the Poem

time_bands.activity: Students open the textbook to the poem. The teacher reads the complete poem once at a natural, expressive pace with the class following. A second reading has the class joining in fully — choral recitation of all four stanzas.

The teacher assigns each of the four stanzas to a group. Each group practises reading their stanza aloud — attending to phrasing, not just accuracy. After preparation, groups read their stanza in sequence to perform the whole poem.

The teacher reads aloud the lines beginning 'All that you do, / Do with all your might' and asks: 'What is the poet's strongest piece of advice here?' Students discuss in pairs and share responses — the teacher draws out the idea of wholehearted effort versus half-hearted action.

Students read the poem independently and silently, underlining two lines they find most meaningful. Volunteers share their choice and give a one-sentence reason. The teacher collects two or three responses and links the poem's wisdom to everyday student experience.

periods.teacher_notes: Having engaged with the poem's vocabulary and themes in earlier work, students now bring richer understanding to the text. The group-stanza performance naturally distributes voice and allows quieter students to participate within the safety of their group. Independent reading and personal line selection build individual interpretive confidence.

periods.activity_title: One Chapter, One Idea — Whole-Chapter Synthesis

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes 'Work while you work, and play while you play' on the board and asks: 'In one sentence, what is this poem really about?' Students respond orally — the teacher maps the range of answers to show how themes of focus, effort, and balance run through every part of the chapter.

Vocabulary round-up: the teacher calls out 'might', 'useful', 'moments', and then 'calm', 'chalk', 'talk' — students give the meaning for the first three and demonstrate the silent-l for the second group, blending word-meaning and phonics knowledge from across the chapter.

Retelling challenge: in pairs, Student A retells the poem's message in their own words (not recitation — explanation). Student B adds one sentence about the Madhubani painting and what it shows about people doing many things with full attention. Partners switch roles.

Quick independent writing: students write three to four sentences in their notebooks titled 'What I do with all my might'. The prompt invites them to connect the poem's idea to their own daily experience — a short, self-contained piece that begins and ends here.

Closing choral recitation of the full poem, followed by one student sharing their written sentences aloud. The teacher closes by naming the chapter's central invitation — to do one thing at a time, and do it well — as a transferable habit, not just a poem's lesson.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis brings together the poem's language, the vocabulary of focus and effort, the silent-l phonics, the Madhubani picture's lesson about purposeful activity, and the riddles' patience — each named by its content, not by which unit taught it. The independent writing is short and self-contained so every student finishes within the time available.

items.source_context: Poem on focus, effort, balance; end-rhyme pairs play/way, might/right, well/tell, away/play.
items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 36 beginning "Things done by halves". What does the poet mean by 'things done by halves'?

options.label: A
options.text: Tasks that take only half the time to finish.

options.label: B
options.text: Tasks that are not completed with full effort or attention.

options.label: C
options.text: Tasks that two people share equally between them.

options.label: D
options.text: Tasks that are easy and need very little work.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Students who choose this focus on the word 'half' as a time measure rather than a quality of effort.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals a literal reading of 'halves' as division between people rather than incomplete effort.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests the student has confused an easy task with a half-hearted one, missing the poem's warning.

items.source_lo: Student infers theme and identifies sound-patterns using a didactic poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Poem on focus, effort, balance; end-rhyme pairs play/way, might/right, well/tell, away/play.
items.item_stem: The poem uses end-rhyme to reinforce its message. Name two pairs of rhyming words from the poem and explain in one or two sentences how the repeating refrain 'work while you work, and play while you play' connects to the poem's central idea.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Acceptable rhyming pairs include play/way, might/right, well/tell, and away/play. The repeating refrain reinforces the poem's central idea that work and play each deserve full attention — by returning to the same words, the poet makes the message memorable and insistent.

items.item_stem:
Read the sentence below and complete the blank with the correct word.
Every morning I ________ my teeth, eat breakfast, and then leave for school.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: brush (or clean). The sentence describes a morning routine activity that fits the daily-routine theme of the chapter's writing task.

items.item_stem: Write a short paragraph of three to four sentences about what you do after school. Use time words like 'first', 'then', and 'after that' to connect your sentences. Your paragraph should show at least one activity that is work and one that is play.

expected_elements: Uses at least two time-order connectives correctly.
Names one work activity and one play activity.
Writes three or more connected sentences.
